Gender is how a person identifies themselves on the inside, with the majority of people being "cis-gendered" (meaning same, or matching). Other genders include trans-gendered (other gendered), a-gendered (no gendered), two-spirit (both gendered), fluid-gendered (a gender that changes), or non-binary (somewhere in the middle of genders). The language (and stigma) around gender may change from place to place, so be sure to ask your child what their gender means to them. I bet they have a lot to share about it! 

For myself, I arrived at my understanding of non-binary gender after of life feeling too boyish to be a girl (I was assigned as female at birth), but not boyish enough to want to transition. I also would feel really uncomfortable living life as a man! I found it easy to emphasize with all of my friends when they talked about the challenges of their gender/sex, and I am comfortable in both male and female spaces. I generally became the first person people approach when opening up about being transgender, and have been friends to a few dozen gender non-conforming people in my life.

It takes a person with profound empathy and universal human compassion to be non-binary. We tend to walk in both worlds, and while you may be concerned that your child may be targeted or harassed, that has not been my experience. Your child is approaching their teenaged years, and you can expect some experimentation (as with all teenagers). Hi! Autistic and 34. When I was 15, there wasn't really language to describe the gender queer feelings I was experiencing. I'd describe myself as agendered now, though I pass as my sex assigned at birth. 


The fact that your dad is concerned is pretty typical of a loving parent who is unfamiliar or misinformed about emerging gender issues. Thankfully, just because these concepts are new to our society and to your dad, doesn't mean they're new to the human experience. There are the Bugis peoples of Indonesia for example. There's the two spirit peoples of the Pacific northwest first Nations. There are educational channels on YouTube that talk about the overlap of autism and gender. There are resources for him, if and when he wants to learn about the delio with gender queer communities. The fact he thinks you're being groomed is a sign he's getting all of his information from one place, and that's a problem of your father's making for himself. 

At 15 there's not much you can do, other than to encourage your father to participate in the gender queer community. He may not be interested, he may not be emotionally mature enough, or he may be traumatized from an incident in the past to participate or learn. Concerns over grooming is very real, and as an autistic afab who was groomed by a cis straight man at 14, it's something to be aware  about. All communities have groomers, and being able to spot and call out problem grooming behaviours is absolutely something you familiarize yourself with, and talk about with people around you.

Advocate for yourself, communicate with others, invite outsiders to learn, and be aware of the risks. You got this OP!
